item.title: Attenuation of shoaling extreme wave crests by artificial salt marshes
item.description: arXiv:2610.36148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laboratory experiments in a wave flume investigated the attenuation of shoaling extreme waves by artificial salt marshes placed immediately before an abrupt depth transition. Increasing vegetation density systematically reduced the excess kurtosis of the surface elevation distribution in the intermediate water depth regime. Nonetheless, attenuation exhibits a short saturation regime at low vegetation densities, whereas at very high densities, excess kurtosis decreases significantly across the gauges. However, kurtosis attenuation becomes ineffective as waves approach shallow-water conditions or as second-order nonlinear effects become significant. Furthermore, the highest experimental densities where the kurtosis is tamed exceed typical natural salt marsh stem densities. Thus, in natural settings, salt marshes are likely to provide only partial mitigation of extreme wave statistics in intermediate and shallow water depths, as the wave field retains some hazardous nonlinearity.
item.dc:creator: Zachary Quek, Sahana Mahesh, Martin Fronty, Seungo Baek, Gun Kim, Saulo Mendes

item.title: Two-layer conjugate flows in an open channel
item.description: arXiv:2610.36242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate conjugate flows in a two-layer fluid system with a flat bottom and a free surface. These are up- and downstream states consistent with simultaneous conservation of mass, momentum, and energy; and therefore candidate end-states of one-dimensional dissipationless bores. By choosing variables in a specific way, we are able to explicitly parameterize all physical non-trivial conjugate flows in the system, using only rational functions. This two-parameter family can be categorized according to whether the states are compatible with (1) a rising surface, and falling internal interface; or (2) vice versa. In particular, we rule out the existence of monotone bore solutions, consistent with an earlier result due to Chen, Walsh, and Wheeler. However, here we do so already at the level of conjugate flows. Separating these two distinct categories is a one-parameter family of critical trivial conjugate flows. The complete description obtained in the present paper serves as an important stepping stone towards finding actual realizing heteroclinic orbits connecting such conjugate states.
item.dc:creator: Robin Ming Chen, Kristoffer Varholm, Annie Grace Wang

item.title: DSMC Study of Hypersonic Boundary-Layer Unsteadiness Using Data-Driven Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.36248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The prediction of transition remains challenging because the receptivity amplitude is usually prescribed rather than measured. This work uses Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) to study an unforced Mach 6 nitrogen boundary layer over a 120 mm flat plate, with no imposed inlet wave, wall signal, modal shape, or disturbance spectrum. The retained unsteady field is the intrinsic finite-particle stochastic fluctuation field carried by the DSMC representation. Changing the DSMC particle count provides an independent numerical control parameter that sets a predictable finite-particle noise floor while preserving the time-averaged boundary-layer flow. Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) is then applied to unforced DSMC snapshots. The DMD eigenvalues and spatial modes estimate the quantities that appear in the LST normal-mode description, including frequency, temporal growth or decay, wavenumber, wavelength, phase speed, mode location, and amplification envelope. LST is used after extraction to test whether the data-derived structures occupy the expected second-mode band. The results show that DSMC data can connect a measured finite-particle stochastic disturbance level to second-mode instability dynamics without imposed disturbance spectra.
item.dc:creator: Mert Senkardesler, Irmak T. Karpuzcu, Deborah A. Levin, Vassilis Theofilis

item.title: Submerged Immiscible Oil Jet: Breakup Dynamics and Droplet Size Modelling
item.description: arXiv:2610.36439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Immiscible liquid-liquid jets occur in numerous industrial and environmental settings, including oil spill response and liquid-liquid extraction, yet the coupled evolution of turbulence, interfacial instability, and droplet size distribution across transitional to turbulent regimes remains poorly understood. We present a combined experimental and theoretical investigation of a silicone oil jet injected into refractive-index-matched sugar water, employing simultaneous Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Planar Laser-Induced Fluorescence (PLIF). Beyond the breakup region, mean velocity and Reynolds stress profiles exhibit self-similarity. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) of the volume fraction reveals a systematic shift in the dominant instability mechanism with increasing Reynolds number: axisymmetric Rayleigh-Plateau modes govern breakup at low Reynolds numbers, sinuous and varicose modes coexist in the transitional regime, and Kelvin-Helmholtz-driven shear-layer breakup dominates at higher Reynolds numbers. Droplet sizes are extracted from PLIF images using a convolutional neural network-based segmentation approach. In the transitional regime, a bimodal droplet size distribution is observed, reflecting the coexistence of shear-induced breakup and Rayleigh-Plateau instability. As the Reynolds number increases and turbulent dissipation intensifies, the distribution evolves toward a single mode with smaller characteristic droplet sizes. To predict the droplet size distribution, existing population balance models are extended to include droplet coalescence. Incorporating coalescence substantially improves agreement with experimental measurements, particularly for larger droplets. These findings demonstrate that turbulent dissipation, interfacial instabilities, and droplet coalescence collectively govern the evolution of droplet size distribution in immiscible liquid-liquid jets.
item.dc:creator: Lokendra Mohan Sharma, Aditya K. Aiyer, Harish N. Dixit, Lakshmana Dora Chandrala

item.title: FAMIR: Future-aligned latent dynamics for complex-flow forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.36515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learned flow surrogates are applied recursively, so errors in phase, amplitude and transport accumulate as each prediction feeds the next. During training, however, the realized next state is known. We propose Future-Aligned Motion Inference for Recursive Physical Forecasting (FAMIR), which uses this realized future to shape the signal that drives the update, not only the predicted state. On the latent grid of a frozen autoencoder, a future-conditioned teacher and a history-only student infer motion tensors that condition one shared residual transition. Posterior--Prior Motion Alignment (PPMA) jointly aligns the teacher (posterior) and student (prior) motions, prediction-fed multistep objectives train the student on its own rollouts, and only the student is deployed. On viscoelastic channel flow, Rayleigh--B\'enard convection and planetary shallow-water flow, FAMIR achieves lower complete-prefix normalized root-mean-square error than three direct latent predictors of comparable size and a delay-embedded linear reference at ten steps (1.003\%, 1.055%, 0.620%) and twenty steps (1.661%, 1.683%, 1.036%). Its advantage is largest at the first step in the viscoelastic flow and grows with lead time in the other flows. Over forty-step forecasts, FAMIR keeps fluctuation profiles and probability densities closer to the reference than the direct predictors. Without the teacher, the motion-conditioned student already outperforms the direct predictors; in the shallow-water flow, prediction-fed rollouts are decisive and joint alignment is far more effective than distillation toward a fixed teacher (1.036% against 1.874%). Fixed-state interventions show that the trained update relies on the state-specific motion, and the deployed student matches the one-step accuracy of the future-informed teacher.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Chen, Yan Wang, Haotian Cheng, Hongna Zhang, Wenhua Zhang, Yuke Li, Xiaobin Li, Fengchen Li

item.title: Rotation-driven suppression and re-emergence of unsteady flow past a circular cylinder
item.description: arXiv:2610.36556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The flow past a rotating cylinder undergoes substantial changes in its wake dynamics and aerodynamic response with increasing rotation rate. This study investigates these changes in two-dimensional compressible flow at \(Re_\infty=3800\) and \(M_\infty=0.1\), with the rotation rate systematically varied over \(0.1\leq\Omega\leq10\) using 130 high-fidelity simulations. At low rotation rates, conventional periodic vortex shedding is progressively suppressed with increasing rotation. A narrow transition regime around \(\Omega=2.2-2.8\) is identified, where sustained oscillations evolve into intermittent fluctuations before reaching a nearly quiescent state. At higher rotation rates, unsteadiness re-emerges with distinctly intermittent and multiscale characteristics, demonstrating that this instability is fundamentally different from conventional K\'arm\'an shedding. The surface pressure and streamwise skin-friction distributions reveal substantial redistribution of aerodynamic loading with rotation, characterized by increasingly intense suction and significant modification of the near-wall shear field. The maximum lift increases systematically with rotation, reflecting the strengthening Magnus-Robins effect, whereas drag exhibits a non-monotonic response with enhanced variability at high rotation rates. Despite the low free-stream Mach number, rotational acceleration produces local Mach numbers approaching 0.5, indicating appreciable compressibility effects in the near-cylinder region. Vorticity-based proper orthogonal decomposition further reveals a transition from wake-dominated coherent structures at low rotation to strongly wrapped, rotation-dominated structures at high rotation. These results establish a direct connection between rotational forcing, surface loading, compressibility, and the suppression and subsequent re-emergence of flow unsteadiness.
item.dc:creator: Aditi Sengupta, Sanjeev Kumar, Puneet Kumar

item.title: Multiple-relaxation-time total enthalpy lattice Boltzmann model for liquid-vapor phase change
item.description: arXiv:2610.36575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, a multiple-relaxation-time (MRT) total enthalpy lattice Boltzmann (LB) model is proposed for liquid-vapor phase change. The pseudopotential LB method is employed to describe the liquid-vapor multiphase dynamics, while the thermal field is solved using an MRT LB formulation with total enthalpy as the evolution variable, thereby incorporating sensible and latent heat into a unified framework. A latent heat expression based on the equation of state (EOS) is further derived to provide a thermodynamic reference for its specification. Multiscale analysis demonstrates that the proposed model recovers the target macroscopic energy equation without introducing the nonlinear thermodynamic source term commonly required in temperature-based formulations, thereby avoiding the explicit evaluation of $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}$. The model is validated through free droplet evaporation, droplet evaporation on a heated surface, and bubble growth and departure during boiling, showing good agreement with published results. Simulations with different prescribed latent heats are further conducted in all three cases, demonstrating that the latent heat can be independently specified according to the physical conditions considered without altering the equation of state.
item.dc:creator: Hangyu He, Lei Wang, Xuguang Yang, Yong Zhao

item.title: A regularized lattice Boltzmann model for the solid-liquid phase change
item.description: arXiv:2610.36642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, a regularized lattice Boltzmann method is proposed for solid-liquid phase-change simulations. The governing total-enthalpy equation is solved within a regularized lattice Boltzmann (RLB) framework, which enables accurate tracking of the solid-liquid interface while effectively suppressing numerical diffusion. In addition, the multi-relaxation-time RLB (MRT-RLB) model with standard lattices is developed to solve the flow field. To enhance computational efficiency, an efficient multi-GPU (graphics processing unit) implementation based on CUDA C (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is developed, which is particularly suited for computationally intensive three-dimensional phase-change simulations. The proposed model is validated against a series of one-, two-, and three-dimensional benchmark problems. The results demonstrate that the present solver provides a robust, accurate, and efficient framework for simulating solid-liquid phase-change heat transfer.
item.dc:creator: Qiang Fu, Yu Han, Xuhui Li, Xiaowen Shan

item.title: Learning the solution operator of standing waves with a Fourier neural operator
item.description: arXiv:2610.36747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The standing wave problem concerns the space-time periodic motion at the free surface of a two-dimensional, infinitely deep, irrotational flow of an incompressible inviscid fluid under gravity. Although spectrally accurate computations have revealed a rich array of nonlinear wave phenomena, repeatedly evaluating their evolution over large parameter spaces remains challenging, particularly when resolving fine-scale spatial oscillations. We employ a Fourier neural operator (FNO) architecture to learn the solution operator along a numerically computed one-parameter family of symmetric standing waves. Given a wave profile at an instant of rest and a normalized observation time, the learned operator predicts the fluid surface, the velocity potential and the dipole density at the surface at that time. In-distribution tests yield uniformly small relative errors within the training range. Two out-of-distribution experiments characterize extrapolation toward contrasting physical regimes. Toward the free-fall limit, errors concentrate near the sharpening crest, consistent with the spectral truncation in the FNO architecture. Toward the linear limit, absolute errors remain small whereas relative errors increase as the amplitude vanishes. A residual of the governing equations, evaluated independently of reference solutions, complements these tests and provides a diagnostic for exploratory predictions beyond the available data.
item.dc:creator: Changhong Mou, Savana Ammons, Di Qi, Vera Mikyoung Hur

item.title: Wall modes in rotating penetrative internally heated convection
item.description: arXiv:2610.36928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rotating internally heated convection has been studied almost exclusively in laterally periodic domains, which cannot support the sidewall-attached modes that appear for sufficient rotation rates in rotating Rayleigh--B\'enard convection in containers. We conduct direct numerical simulations of internally heated convection with isothermal plates and an adiabatic sidewall in cylinders of aspect ratio $\Gamma = 1/2$, $1$, and $2$ at $\Ra = 10^8$ and $\Pran = 1$, comparing them with a doubly periodic layer. When rotation is strong enough to stabilise the flow in a doubly periodic layer at the same $R$ ($\Ek \lessapprox 2 \times 10^{-5}$), the cylinders continue transporting heat via a wall mode down to $\Ek = 5.62 \times 10^{-6}$. This mode consists of a wave attached to the sidewall, with a radial thickness of roughly $0.03$ layer depths independent of $\Gamma$, leaving a stationary interior. Although unstable stratification is confined to the upper half of the conductive state, the mode also penetrates the lower half while retaining stable mean stratification in the measured lower-layer interval. Its azimuthal wavenumber scales roughly with $\Gamma$, yielding a wall parallel wavelength on the order of the layer depth, and it drifts retrograde as a rigid wave slower in wider cylinders and at lower $\Ek$. Analogous to rotating Rayleigh--B\'enard convection, the wall modes reported here extend the observed range of sustained convection relative to the periodic reference and may complicate experimental comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel A. Tarditti, Rodolfo Ostilla-M\'onico, Ali Arslan

item.title: Local Metrics for Exact Streaming on Curvilinear Lattices: A Curvilinear D3Q27 Cumulant Lattice-Boltzmann Method
item.description: arXiv:2610.36971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A three-dimensional curvilinear lattice-Boltzmann method is introduced for simulations on smoothly deformed grids while retaining exact one-to-one streaming on a uniform computational lattice. The coordinate transformation is represented locally through a metric-Gaussian equilibrium and a Christoffel-connection source in moment space. A dynamically reconstructed homogeneous-state perturbation streaming procedure preserves homogeneous physical states on warped meshes without interpolation in the advection step. The method is implemented on a D3Q27 lattice with a cumulant collision operator, while the geometric construction remains compatible with other local collision models. The formulation is assessed using two sets of tests. First, static non-orthogonal warped-cube cases validate the bulk curvilinear solver through a convected helical shear wave, the Taylor--Green vortex, and Arnold--Beltrami--Childress flow. These tests verify viscous decay, clean freestream preservation, vortex-breakdown dynamics, and the nonlinear inertial--pressure balance induced by geometric acceleration. Second, wall-bounded and moving-boundary demonstrations assess the boundary-compatible extension through warped plane Poiseuille flow, arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) peristaltic pumping, and a two-way fluid--structure interaction (FSI) case with added-mass frequency shift. The results show that the proposed curvilinear LBM avoids interpolation-based transport, reduces geometry-locked numerical modes, preserves global mass and momentum to round-off accuracy in the tested warped periodic cases, and extends to wall-bounded ALE/FSI configurations with conservative treatment of mass and physically consistent momentum exchange.
item.dc:creator: Maher Sawaf, Jonas Latt, Nikolaus A. Adams, Mostafa S. Shadloo

item.title: DSMC Study on Unsteadiness of Supersonic Flow Over a Cylinder
item.description: arXiv:2610.37048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unsteady flow over a 30 $\mu$m diameter cylinder at Mach 4 is investigated using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo across Reynolds numbers from 270 to 6750, spanning slip-flow to near-continuum regimes. Power Spectral Density analysis at discrete probe locations and Dynamic Mode Decomposition of flowfield snapshots independently characterize instabilities in both the stagnation and wake regions. In the stagnation region, a bow shock pulsation mode at 10-15 MHz frequency is identified across all cases despite a 24-fold variation in number density. In the wake, two distinct instabilities are observed. The canonical vortex shedding mode at Strouhal number St $\approx$ 0.2 dominates at lower Reynolds numbers. A second instability at St $\approx$ 0.5, consistent with previously reported slipline-driven oscillations in supersonic wakes, emerges at higher Reynolds numbers and progressively strengthens, becoming the dominant mode. In the studied Reynolds range, the wake transitions from no clear unsteadiness, to canonical vortex shedding at St $\approx$ 0.20, and reaching a regime where the St $\approx$ 0.5 mode becomes dominant, while also having a distinct independent bow shock pulsation possibly governed by its standoff distance.
item.dc:creator: Mert Senkardesler, Irmak T. Karpuzcu, Deborah A. Levin

item.title: Mode-2 solitary waves in continuous stratifications
item.description: arXiv:2610.37289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computed herein are examples of mode-2 internal solitary waves to the Dubreil-Jacotin-Long (DJL) equation. These are localised, fully nonlinear waves in a continuously stratified, inviscid fluid under the Boussinesq and rigid-lid approximations. The equation is solved directly using finite differences on a periodic domain, enabling the computation of both generalised solitary waves, which possess oscillatory mode-1 tails, and embedded solitary waves, whose tails vanish. Two stratifications are considered. The first is a double pycnocline, generalising the three-layer system considered by Doak et al. (2022) by replacing each infinitesimal interface with a pycnocline of finite thickness. The second stratification, a surface mixed layer above an exponentially stratified layer, shows that embedded mode-2 solitary waves are not restricted to double-pycnocline stratifications. These are the first mode-2 solitary waves of the DJL equation computed for stratifications that are asymmetric about mid-depth.
item.dc:creator: Alex Doak, Ricardo Barros, Paul l A. Milewski

item.title: Free-vortex-wake dynamics of airborne wind energy kites in crosswind flight
item.description: arXiv:2610.37313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The wake of an airborne wind energy kite is shaped by its crosswind path and, for on-board generation, by the slipstreams of its rotors, and in farms it reaches downstream units. It is computed here by a vortex step method with a time-marching free vortex wake, implemented by the authors in their open-source code OpenFAWE with a lumped-mass tether, actuator-disc rotors releasing vortex rings and several kites. It reproduces an independent vortex step code to 10^-9 on the rigid-wing Makani M600 and within 0.3% in lift and 0.9% in drag on the TU Delft V3 leading-edge inflatable kite, matching its Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes lift within 3.1%. For fixed kites the lift deficit of a finite wake is the far field of its starting vortex, which fixes the wake length before a run, and the vortex core must stay below the narrowest panel width. With these settings the helical tip-vortex pair of the M600 on its loop lowers its lift by about 0.5% from 5 to 13 m/s. Free rotor rings do not converge with the time step, whereas an undeformed slipstream tube converges once its rings are refined at the wing and raises the lift by 1.9%. A slipstream deflected by the wing lowers it by 3.5%, so the treatment near the wing sets the sign of the rotor effect. A second unit one loop diameter downstream loses 0.5% of its lift and 2.2% of its aerodynamic power, with or without rotors.
item.dc:creator: Yinong Tian, Shan Wang

item.title: Spatial Colorimetric Mapping of pH and Dissolved Carbon during Convective Dissolution of CO{\_2}: Constraints from Domain, Geometry, and Indicator Mix on Measurement Reliability
item.description: arXiv:2610.37335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying the dissolution and buoyancy-driven transport of CO2-rich water is critical to understanding solubility trapping mechanism in geologic storage. Analog-fluid density driven convection experiments do not represent CO2 dissolution chemistry or the aqueous CO2 density-concentration monotonic relationship. X-ray tomography does not provide enough contrast to directly measure dissolved CO2. Spatial colorimetry provides an inexpensive method to map pH and estimate total dissolved inorganic carbon (CT) via carbonate equilibrium assumptions. However, the effects of experimental conditions such as domain (free fluid and porous), geometry (2D and 3D), and indicator mix concentration on the reliability of pH and CT measurements remain unexplored. We evaluated how these factors affect the reliability of measurements using two different colorimetric models (hue and spherical coordinates ({\theta} and {\phi})). Hue was reliable in all domains whereas {\theta}-{\phi} was reliable in free fluid. Lower indicator mix concentration increased the chromatic sensitivity at low pH in free fluid; however, it did not produce sufficient color contrast for pH calibration and mapping in the porous domain. In the porous domain, {\theta}-{\phi} calibration was 33 times more susceptible to noise than hue. Temporal pH noise was less than 0.01 units; spatial noise changed domain-mean CT by 0.6-4.4{\%}. Both models were able to resolve CO2-rich plumes in free fluid; however, {\theta}-{\phi} had sharper plume boundaries than hue. The temporal evolution of CO2 dissolution resolved by the color models agreed more in 2D than 3D. These findings provide a reliability framework for studying subsurface dissolution and mixing of CO2.
item.dc:creator: Joe-sam Nkuah, Vance Sisson, Haochen Li, Anna Herring

item.title: Development and assessment of a target-$\omega$ interfacial turbulence-damping model for stratified gas--liquid flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.37376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interfacial turbulence damping is required in Reynolds-averaged simulations of stratified gas--liquid flows when strong interfacial velocity gradients are present. In this work, we develop a target-$\omega$ interfacial damping formulation for the low-Reynolds-number Wilcox-type $k$--$\omega$ model in a one-field RANS/VOF framework. A gas-side target value of the specific dissipation rate $\omega$ is constructed from an effective interfacial wall coordinate determined from the local resolved flow. The constructed target-$\omega$ provides a smooth transition between the viscous and logarithmic limits through power-law blending and requires no calibration of model constants against target data. \textcolor{black}{The formulation is first assessed against three gas-layer DNS cases at $Re_\tau\simeq180$ with different interface velocities. The model reproduces the principal features of the mean velocity, turbulent kinetic energy and Reynolds shear-stress distributions, while showing substantially weaker sensitivity to the near-interface grid resolution than the Egorov-type formulation, although some grid dependence remains on the coarsest mesh. The assessment is then extended to the co-current Fabre stratified-flow experiment at a higher Reynolds number and to the counter-current St\"abler experiment}. In both cases, the present formulation provides generally good predictions of the gas-side mean flow and turbulence statistics without case-specific adjustment. For the St\"abler case, in which the liquid level develops as part of the coupled two-phase solution, the predicted mean liquid depth agrees closely with the measured value. These results indicate that the target-$\omega$ formulation provides a consistent interfacial turbulence-damping treatment for resolved large gas--liquid interfaces over the range of conditions considered.
item.dc:creator: Di Wu, Junda Liu, Qiaopeng Wang, Liu Liu, Dongling Wu, Ping Zhou, Pengyu Shi

item.title: A Systematic Assessment of Artificial Flame Thickening for Thermodiffusively Unstable Lean Hydrogen Flames in Homogeneous Isotropic Turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.37577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Artificially Thickened Flame (ATF) approach is widely used to render premixed flames resolvable on coarse computational meshes, but thickening alters their interaction with turbulence. While considerable research has focused on the effects of thickening on turbulence-induced flame wrinkling, its influence on the mean local flame propagation speed in turbulent, thermodiffusively unstable hydrogen flames remains poorly understood. More than 200 flame-resolved simulations of premixed flames in homogeneous isotropic turbulence with detailed chemistry and transport are used to systematically isolate and quantify the effects of artificial thickening. Thickening the flame by a factor $F$ increases its effective flame-scale Karlovitz number according to $Ka_{\mathrm{f}}^F = Ka_{\mathrm{f}}\sqrt{F}$, while decreasing its effective Damk\"ohler number according to $Da_{\mathrm{f}}^F = Da_{\mathrm{f}}/F$. In the regime considered here, the former enhances the mean local flame speed, whereas the latter reduces flame wrinkling, resulting in opposing effects on the flame consumption speed; hence, changes in both local flame propagation and flame area must be accounted for. Simulations matched with respect to $Ka_{\mathrm{f}}^F$ and $Da_{\mathrm{f}}^F$ collapse across different thickening factors $F$ until the thickened flame approaches the integral or geometric length scales of the configuration. Based on these scaling relations, a self-consistent efficiency correction is proposed to recover the unthickened flame consumption speed. Since the efficiency factor feeds back on the effective Karlovitz and Damk\"ohler numbers, it must be determined implicitly.
item.dc:creator: Max Schneider, Vinzenz Schuh, Felix Rong, Driss Kaddar, Andrew J. Aspden, Thomas L. Howarth, Christian Hasse, Hendrik Nicolai

item.title: Continuum thermodynamics of chemically reacting multi-temperature fluid mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2610.37637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a continuum-thermodynamic model for chemically reacting, multi-velocity and multi-temperature fluid mixtures. Partial balances of mass, momentum and total energy are closed using a single entropy density depending jointly on the constituent mass and nonkinetic internal-energy densities. Its partial derivatives determine the constituent temperatures and chemical potentials. For the chosen entropy flux and separately treated volume deformation, the strengthened entropy principle yields a weighted Euler relation constraining the partial thermodynamic pressures. We construct thermodynamically consistent constitutive relations for viscosity, heat conduction, Maxwell--Stefan momentum exchange, thermal relaxation and nonlinear reaction kinetics. The baseline model includes thermo-diffusion and its reciprocal coupling; a fully coupled reciprocal completion is given within the stated isotropic co-factor class. An alternative formulation couples chemical conversion and energy redistribution through specified elementary processes. We identify the material functions required for closure and admissible shifts of constituent energy zeros. An ionization network with resolved electronic levels yields Saha-type ionization relations and Boltzmann excitation ratios under the stated detailed-balance assumptions, recovering the Saha--Eggert relation at common temperature. Competing electron- and heavy-particle processes can maintain stationary populations while transferring energy between groups at different prescribed temperatures.
item.dc:creator: Dieter Bothe, Tommaso Ruggeri

item.title: A Graph-informed Kriging model for sample-efficient Bayesian optimization of wind farm layouts
item.description: arXiv:2610.35975v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wind farm layout optimization becomes increasingly difficult as turbine count grows, especially when high-fidelity aerodynamic models are used. Conventional Kriging-based Bayesian optimization often suffers from low sample efficiency in high-dimensional layout spaces because sparse training data provide limited domain coverage. We develop a Graph-informed Kriging framework that embeds reusable aerodynamic interaction information into the surrogate mean function. The wind farm is represented as a directed aerodynamic graph, where pairwise turbine interactions defined in a low-dimensional relative-coordinate space are assembled into a farm-scale mean. This structured mean captures the dominant variation in annual energy production (AEP), allowing the Gaussian process to model only the residual structure and uncertainty. Numerical experiments show that Graph-informed Kriging consistently improves AEP prediction accuracy over ordinary and generic-trend Kriging under sparse-data conditions, with increasing benefits as layout dimension and wake-interaction strength grow. Embedded in Bayesian optimization, it substantially improves sample efficiency and achieves competitive solutions for the IEA Wind Task 37 benchmark with about 280 AEP evaluations. In a controlled 16-turbine case, it also outperforms ordinary and multi-fidelity Kriging under the same high-fidelity evaluation budget. The framework is further extended to a 48-turbine wind farm, demonstrating applicability to large-scale CFD-based layout optimization. These results show that Graph-informed surrogate modeling can enable more efficient use of high-fidelity aerodynamic models for reliable large-scale wind farm layout design.
item.dc:creator: Zhen-Fan Wang, Kai Zhang, Xianping Du, Zhaolong Han, Dai Zhou, Onur Bilgen

item.title: Cutting, Shuffling and Diffusion as a Coarsening Process
item.description: arXiv:2610.35979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cutting and shuffling (CS) rearranges fluid without stretching, but homogenisation requires diffusion (D); this interaction is not well understood. We show that CSD is a coarsening process, with scale $\bar\ell=L(n_c\mathrm{Pe}/2)^{-1/3}$ rather than the Batchelor scale, and that cutting acts as a fractional Laplacian in wavenumber, giving the exact mixing rate $\gamma=2^{1/3}|a_1'|n_c^{2/3}\lambda\mathrm{Pe}^{-1/3}$ for $n_c$ cuts per event at rate $\lambda$, with $a_1'=-1.0188\dots$ the first zero of $\mathrm{Ai}'$. This holds in any dimension for random and deterministic protocols, extends to finite-time mixing, and places CSD in a known non-equilibrium universality class.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Lester, Tanguy LeBorgne, Joris Heyman

item.title: Quantum hydrodynamics from Nambu's unpublished fluid notes
item.description: arXiv:2610.36275v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a quantum hydrodynamic theory based on Nambu's unpublished note \emph{A New Look at Fluid Dynamics}. The kinetic action defines a metric on configuration space and a mechanical connection coupling an observable cyclic deformation to unobserved fluid modes. Tracing out these modes yields a quantum channel for the observed deformation. We establish a criterion for the exact preservation of coherence between opposite momenta and show how nonzero connection curvature prevents this coupling from being removed. The leading quadratic decay of quantum coherence is determined by the prepared quantum state. For two shear flows, we identify an exact noiseless sign subsystem. Introducing additional generating flows cancels the initial residual of the Euler equations while producing nonzero connection curvature, governed by the same kinetic integrals that determine the classical correction. At fixed mean energy, choosing amplitudes adapted to the dominant coupling flow substantially reduces the initial decoherence, even along the direction that cancels the Euler residual. This advantage gradually diminishes under conditional evolution, eventually leading to a crossing of the decoherence curves. Our example shows that a preparation with a smaller initial coherence-decay coefficient can have a larger maximum sampled loss over a finite readout interval.
item.dc:creator: Kazuki Ikeda

item.title: High-Fidelity Aerostructural Dataset of Transonic Wings in Cruise Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.36442v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have the potential to substantially accelerate aircraft wing design, a process that has traditionally required extensive high-fidelity simulation and design iteration. Existing public datasets for ML-based wing design have focused primarily on aerodynamic performance, with limited consideration of the multidisciplinary interactions that govern practical aircraft design. In particular, efficient wing design requires simultaneous consideration of aerodynamic performance and structural integrity, yet no publicly available datasets capture this coupled aerostructural behavior at high-fidelity. To address this need, a high-fidelity multidisciplinary dataset for static aerostructural analysis of transonic wings is introduced. The dataset includes 2471 samples, along with three out-of-distribution samples. The wing planform geometry is parameterized by span, sweep, dihedral, tip chord, and tip twist, while the airfoil cross-sections are parameterized using the class-shape transformation method. The analysis is further parameterized by Mach number, angle of attack, altitude, and structural load factor. The utility of the dataset is demonstrated by training state-of-the-art ML models to predict aerodynamic surface quantities, integrated aerodynamic performance quantities, and the failure distribution of the wingbox. ML models achieve at most 0.0309 normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) in the prediction of aerodynamic quantities and at most 0.1189 NRMSE in the prediction of failure distribution of the wingbox. By providing coupled aerodynamic and structural responses for a diverse set of transonic wings, this dataset establishes a benchmark for developing, evaluating, and comparing multi-physics ML models for wing design. Broadly, it is intended to encourage creation of similar high-fidelity multi-physics benchmark datasets across engineering domains.
item.dc:creator: Pavankumar Koratikere, Abhijnan Dikshit, Leifur Leifsson

item.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.36888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FAST.Farm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.
item.dc:creator: Mart\'in de Frutos, Baptiste Corban, Claire Bizon Monroc, Ana Bu\v{s}i\'c, Donatien Dubuc, Jiamin Zhud, Esteban Ferrer

item.title: Hydrodynamic fluctuations in Luttinger liquids
item.description: arXiv:2610.37301v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop the theory of hydrodynamic fluctuations for one-dimensional quantum liquids. At low temperatures the relaxation of interacting electrons in a single-channel wire separates into two classes: equilibration, which changes the numbers of right and left movers through backscattering and is exponentially slow, and thermalization, which redistributes energy and momentum at a fixed number of movers at a power-law rate. This separation of time scales gives the electron liquid a two-fluid description analogous to superfluid $^4$He, with the zero mode of the Luttinger liquid as the superfluid component and the gas of thermal excitations as the normal component. Using Onsager reciprocity and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, we add Langevin fluxes to the two-fluid hydrodynamic equations, including a mutual-friction noise generated by rare backscattering events that has no counterpart in helium. We apply the theory to Coulomb-coupled quantum wires and calculate the dynamic structure factors, which contain a second-sound peak next to the plasmon doublet; the Coulomb drag resistivity, where intrawire equilibration acts as a bottleneck and turns the hydrodynamic drag into an activated temperature dependence; and the near-field heat transfer between the wires. Mode frequencies, spectral weights, linewidths, and the crossover scales of the transport coefficients are expressed through the thermodynamic properties of the liquid and a few dissipative coefficients, providing spectroscopic and transport probes of two-fluid behavior in one-dimensional quantum systems.
item.dc:creator: Alex Levchenko

item.title: Water at the molecular frontier
item.description: arXiv:2610.37581v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Much of the water that matters most - flowing through biological cells and membranes, percolating through soils and rocks, or processed by filtration and desalination technologies - is not bulk water. It is water in nano- and molecular-scale confinement or at interfaces. Nanoscale water is therefore central to many challenges of our time, from the global water crisis and the water-energy nexus to catalysis, electrochemistry, and health. Beyond its applications, nanoscale water has emerged as a rich scientific field in its own right: discoveries are accumulating rapidly, revealing that confinement and interfacial forces produce a range of behaviours absent in the bulk. Sometimes this amounts to a renormalization of bulk properties; in other cases, new and non-intuitive phenomena emerge - exotic phases, anomalous transport, and dielectric responses that defy continuum expectations. A convergence of atomically precise nanofluidic devices, novel spectroscopies and microscopy approaches, and machine-learning-accelerated simulations is now exposing the molecular mechanisms behind these behaviours. This Perspective argues that the recent findings should not be viewed as isolated nanoscale anomalies, but as evidence for a molecular regime of water in which continuum descriptions must be rethought and molecular-level understanding becomes essential. Recognising and exploring this regime should have consequences ranging from fundamental physics to the rational design of future technologies that rely on water and dissolved ions.
item.dc:creator: Mischa Bonn, Marie-Laure Bocquet, Andre Geim, Laura Fumagalli, Angelos Michaelides, Lyderic Bocquet

item.title: Measuring time-resolved heat transfer fluctuations on a heated-thin foil in a turbulent channel airflow
item.description: arXiv:2410.12778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an experimental setup to perform time-resolved convective heat transfer measurements in a turbulent channel flow with air as the working fluid. We employ a heated thin foil coupled with high-speed infrared thermography. The measurement technique is challenged by the thermal inertia of the foil, the high frequency of turbulent fluctuations, and the measurement noise of the infrared camera. We discuss in detail the advantages and drawbacks of all the design choices that were made, thereby providing a successful implementation strategy to obtain high-quality data. This experimental approach could be valuable for studies employing wall-based measurements of turbulence, such as flow control applications in wall-bounded turbulence.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Cu\'ellar, Enrico Amico, Jacopo Serpieri, Gioacchino Cafiero, Woutijn J Baars, Stefano Discetti, Andrea Ianiro

item.title: A Kinetic Study of the Interactions of an Acoustic Vibrating Surface with Hypersonic Boundary-Layer Instabilities
item.description: arXiv:2512.11390v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The response of Mack mode instabilities to a simple acoustic vibrating surface (AVS) is studied using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method to capture and analyze spontaneous second-mode instability growth. The DSMC simulations, analyzed with the Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) method, model flow over a flat plate at an unseeded freestream Mach number of 6 and unit Reynolds number $Re_1\sim 1.18\times10^7$ m$^{-1}$. Power spectral density (PSD) analysis was found to identify the dominant frequencies of 200 to 500 kHz, in line with linear stability theory (LST) predictions. Closed-form kinetic-theory expressions were derived to predict the amplitude of the DSMC fluctuations in the window-averaged snapshots. It was observed that the DSMC-simulated flowfield naturally developed second Mack mode instabilities without any external seeding, i.e., arising spontaneously from the kinetic fluctuations of the simulated gas and of amplitude higher than the predicted DSMC fluctuations. Targeted interaction with these flow instabilities is demonstrated for an AVS, where forcing at the unstable frequency of 250 kHz results in amplified waves downstream, while at the stable frequency of 400 kHz AVS-induced disturbances are damped. The AVS thus excites only the waves at its forcing frequency, leaving the instability waves at other frequencies and the mean flow essentially unaltered. The ability of the kinetic simulations to capture and describe linear perturbations at Reynolds numbers corresponding to those of Mach 6 flight at altitudes of $\sim 20$ km suggests that DSMC provides a theoretical understanding of controlling laminar-turbulent transition through AVS materials in hypersonic boundary layers.
item.dc:creator: Mert Senkardesler, Irmak T. Karpuzcu, Deborah A. Levin

item.title: Differential Geometry of Deterministic Stokesian Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2601.11377v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a differential geometric framework for the motion of a non-Brownian particle in the presence of fixed obstacles in a quiescent fluid, in the deterministic Stokesian regime. While one may think (owing to the Helmholtz Minimum Dissipation Theorem) that the hydrodynamic resistance tensor could be the natural candidate for a Riemannian metric shaping the particle trajectories, we demonstrate that the trajectories driven by constant external forces are \emph{not} geodesics of this bare resistance metric. Instead, they experience a geometric drift due to the curvature induced by the presence of obstacles. By rigorously incorporating translational-rotational coupling through a modified effective resistance tensor $\tilde{\mathbf{R}} = \mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{FU}} - \mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{F\omega}}\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{T\omega}}^{-1}\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{F\omega}}^T$, which accounts for the hidden dissipation savings afforded by particle rotation, we introduce a unified geometric formalism. We prove that the physical particle trajectories are exact geodesics of a conformally scaled metric, $\tilde{g}_{ij} = \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{x})\tilde{R}_{ij}$, where $\mathcal{D}$ is the instantaneous power dissipation. This framework establishes that the affine parameter along the trajectory corresponds strictly to the cumulative energy dissipated. We apply this theory to the scattering of a spherical particle by a fixed spherical obstacle, showing that the exact analytical trajectory derived previously by the author is recovered as a geodesic of the dissipation-scaled manifold.
item.dc:creator: Sumedh R. Risbud

item.title: Iterative Construction of n-Dimensional Navier-Stokes Solutions with Non-Gradient Convection
item.description: arXiv:2609.22372v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exact periodic solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations arise when the convective field is a pure gradient and can be absorbed into the pressure. We construct solutions outside this class, in arbitrary spatial dimension, by an iteration in which each step solves a linear diffusion problem forced by the transverse part of the preceding convective field. The construction is dimension-independent, and for a cyclic family of initial fields the first two iterates are available in closed form. Carried out numerically in three dimensions, the iteration converges: at Re = 10 successive iterates contract with an observed factor 0.43 and the limit is a fixed point of the discretised map to a relative defect of 8.2 x 10^-5. The observed factor exceeds unity by Re = 30, which identifies the practical range of the iteration rather than a proved convergence boundary. We also show what goes wrong when the projection is omitted, as it was in an earlier iteration of the author's: the iterates cease to be divergence-free and an apparent growth appears that belongs to the expansion and not to the flow. For an n-dimensional generalisation of the initial field the fraction of the convective field not absorbed by pressure is exactly 2*sqrt(2)/3 in every dimension n >= 3, and the longitudinal fraction exactly 1/3. The divergence of each returned source is a sharp diagnostic, failing by sixteen orders of magnitude at the step where the projection is omitted; the cell kinetic energy is a weaker one, detecting gross failure only.
item.dc:creator: R. K. Michael Thambynayagam

item.title: CraftSPH: A composable framework for differentiable smoothed particle hydrodynamics implemented in PyTorch
item.description: arXiv:2609.38208v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) is well suited to large-deformation fluid problems, and the growing use of automatic differentiation in engineering applications has motivated interest in differentiable SPH solvers. In this study, a composable differentiable SPH framework, CraftSPH, has been developed. In CraftSPH, major computational operations are implemented as independent modules that users can combine to construct solvers for different purposes. This design supports high-accuracy discretization and both explicit and implicit computation within a common framework, while allowing individual components to be maintained and extended. Selected numerical operations also support automatic differentiation (AD) for physical-parameter estimation and potential coupling with deep learning models. These capabilities were demonstrated through forward and inverse analyses. Forward analyses using an implicit SPH scheme with high-accuracy discretization showed good agreement with analytical and reference solutions for Poiseuille flow and a rising bubble, while capturing the key experimental trends in two- and three-dimensional dam-break problems. In inverse analyses, explicit and implicit SPH schemes were used to estimate kinematic viscosity in Taylor-Green vortex flow and Reynolds number in lid-driven cavity flow. The results also showed that the choice of operations included in the computational graph affects the computed gradients. Together, these findings demonstrate that CraftSPH enables users to assemble problem-specific solvers for forward and inverse analyses within a common framework.
item.dc:creator: Gen Matono, Shujiro Fujioka, Mayuko Nishio

item.title: An Arbitrary-Lagrangian-Eulerian solver for relativistic detonation waves
item.description: arXiv:2606.27113v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper we study the dynamics of relativistic detonation waves theoretically and numerically. The reaction is physically accounted for by an extra term in the definition of the total energy density and by an additional equation for the evolution of the mass fraction of the reactant, while leaving formally unmodified the equations of mass and energy-momentum conservation. In this way, the Rankine-Hugoniot relations maintain the same formal structure of the inert version. For the numerical solution we use a finite volume ALE scheme with a second order TVD space-time reconstruction for the homogeneous part of the system, where the mesh velocity is chosen equal to the shock speed, and we combine it through operator splitting with a locally implicit algorithm for the potentially stiff reaction source terms that arise in the equation of the reactant. We furthermore propose a particularly efficient algorithm for the conversion from the conserved to the primitive variables, which for the relativistic Euler equations is known to be nontrivial. Following this approach, we can successfully solve the Zel'dovich-von Neumann-Doering profile of a relativistic detonation wave, up to Lorentz factors of the shock front $\gamma_s\sim 7$. Our analysis allowed us to highlight a new special relativistic effect, which has remained unnoticed so far. While in Newtonian detonations the Zel'dovich pressure jump decreases monotonically with the mass flux through the shock front, in the relativistic case it shows a minimum and then rises monotonically as a function of the mass flux. This may have interesting physical implications on the amount of energy that can be extracted from a relativistic detonation wave.
item.dc:creator: Sara Rinaldi, Olindo Zanotti, Michael Dumbser

item.title: Odd slip at chiral active surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2609.17005v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Odd slip at solid-liquid interfaces, characterized by a velocity component perpendicular to the applied shear stress, introduces a novel class of odd transport phenomena with transverse momentum transfer at boundaries, distinct from odd viscosity, odd elasticity, or odd diffusivity. This effect arises on chiral active surfaces with persistent energy input and defined handedness, such as carpets of rotating biological or synthetic cilia with flexible anchoring. Although odd slip itself is dissipationless, its maintenance in active systems comes at an energetic cost, which we estimate from the microscopic model. With respect to its orientation dependence, odd slip can be classified as pseudo-scalar or pseudo-vectorial. We use a perturbative expansion to determine the resistance tensors of problems with different levels of broken symmetries. They reveal how the surface chirality and body asymmetry together violate the Onsager symmetry, but uphold the Onsager-Casimir reciprocity. Strikingly, suspensions of particles with odd slip embedded in a conventional Newtonian bulk fluid exhibit odd viscosity, providing a new minimal mechanism for its emergence beyond current microscopic models.
item.dc:creator: Yuto Hosaka, Andrej Vilfan
